aiProse.executiveSummary: This report assesses the feasibility of refurbishing Hargreaves Teaching Block, a three-storey 1960s education building of 1,200 m² at Example University, Birmingham, to provide modern flexible teaching space, replace life-expired services, upgrade fire safety, and improve thermal performance in support of the university's net-zero plan. The estimated total project cost is £1,528,000 to £1,906,000 (excluding VAT), with a confidence grade of Grade A (High Confidence). The target completion date of 1 September 2028 is not achievable from the stated start of 11 January 2027; the 124-week programme completes approximately 38 weeks later, around 28 May 2029. The single most material risk is the requirement to confine all works to vacation windows only, which constrains the construction programme and increases the risk of overrun into term time.
keyFindings: The works cost mid-point is £1,083,000 with a range of £964,000 to £1,202,000, driven primarily by full systems replacement of heating, ventilation, electrical distribution, and fire safety systems across the entire building, together with comprehensive refurbishment of finishes and fittings.

The target date of 1 September 2028 is not achievable; the 124-week programme (including 9 weeks of float) completes around 28 May 2029, approximately 38 weeks beyond the target, and phasing for subsequent phases will extend this further.
The stated budget of £4,500,000 (including fees and unrecovered VAT) is sufficient against the estimated gross range, with headroom of approximately £2,327,000 above the top of the range.

The most significant risk is the requirement to confine works to vacation windows only, which constrains the construction programme and increases the risk of overrun into term time, compounded by asbestos known or suspected in the building and the absence of any services replacement since original construction.

The recommended procurement route is Traditional — Single Stage Tender, which suits this project because formal competitive procurement is required for grant or public funding, and the single-stage approach allows the client design team to maintain design responsibility while achieving cost certainty before construction commences.
scopeAssumptions: The scope includes soft strip of finishes and fittings, windows and external doors, internal doors and ironmongery, wall, floor and ceiling finishes, general fittings and built-in joinery, 120 items of loose furniture and FF&E, sanitary plumbing, IT/data infrastructure, heating and hot water systems, ventilation and air handling, gas installation, electrical distribution and switchgear, electrical wiring, new lighting with occupancy sensors, fire alarm systems, emergency lighting, and M&E overhaul, all measured across the full 1,200 m² of the building.

The roof was recovered in 2011 and windows on the south elevation were replaced in 2016; the north elevation windows remain original, and no services replacement has occurred since the building's original construction in the 1960s, meaning the heating, ventilation, and electrical systems are life-expired and require full replacement.

The building is partially occupied during works, works are confined to vacation windows only, restricted working hours apply, and the site is located in a conservation area or subject to an Article 4 direction, all of which constrain the construction programme and may require enhanced external materials and detailing.
aiProse.costNarrative: The main cost drivers are the full replacement of life-expired mechanical and electrical services across the entire 1,200 m² building, including heating and hot water systems, ventilation and air handling, electrical distribution and switchgear, and fire safety systems, together with comprehensive refurbishment of all internal finishes, fittings, windows, and doors to meet modern teaching standards and net-zero performance targets. The cost is further influenced by the requirement for asbestos management, the conservation area context requiring enhanced external detailing, and the need to maintain restricted working hours and vacation-window-only access throughout the construction phase.
aiProse.roiNarrative: The project cost mid-point is £1,717,000 with an annual benefit of £95,000, yielding a simple payback period of 18.1 years. The key financial risk is that the annual benefit is dependent on achieving the assumed energy and operational cost savings; any shortfall in actual performance or changes to utility costs could extend the payback period and reduce the project's financial return.

constraints.title: Vacation-window-only working
constraints.text: Works must be confined to vacation and holiday periods, which constrains the construction programme to discrete windows and increases the risk of overrun into term time if any phase slips.

constraints.title: Restricted working hours
constraints.text: Restricted working hours apply throughout the project, extending the construction duration and potentially attracting premium or out-of-hours rates that must be confirmed with the client.

constraints.title: Conservation area constraints
constraints.text: The site is in a conservation area or subject to an Article 4 direction, curtailing permitted development rights and likely requiring full planning consent for external alterations and enhanced material specification.

constraints.title: Asbestos management
constraints.text: Asbestos is known or suspected in the building, requiring a valid asbestos register and careful management during soft strip and demolition works to ensure compliance and avoid programme delay.

constraints.title: Life-expired services
constraints.text: No services replacement has occurred since the building's original 1960s construction, meaning heating, ventilation, and electrical systems are life-expired and require complete replacement, which is a significant cost and programme driver.

constraints.title: Target date not achievable
constraints.text: The target completion date of 1 September 2028 is not achievable from the stated start of 11 January 2027; the 124-week programme completes around 28 May 2029, approximately 38 weeks later, and phasing for subsequent phases will extend this further.

nextSteps: Confirm the phasing strategy and the specific vacation windows available for each phase, including blackout dates for examinations (January and May–June), to establish a realistic and achievable programme and agree this with the client and university faculty.

Obtain and review the asbestos register to confirm its currency and scope relevance; if it is a valid R&D survey, it may be reused to reduce the survey programme and risk allowance, potentially saving time on the critical path.

Seek pre-application advice from the local planning authority and conservation officer on the expectations for external alterations, materials, and detailing to avoid delays and cost growth at the planning stage.

Confirm the permitted working hours with the client and university, and price out-of-hours working where programme-critical to the vacation windows, ensuring the Preliminaries allowance reflects the actual site constraints.

Commission or update the condition survey and any other outstanding surveys (structural, M&E, thermal, accessibility) to inform the Stage 2 design and cost plan, and confirm the scope and specification of the heating, ventilation, and electrical systems replacement to achieve net-zero performance targets.

riskRegister.description: Works are confined to vacation windows only; the 124-week programme spans multiple academic terms, creating a high risk of overrun into term time and disruption to teaching activities.
riskRegister.mitigation: Phase works strictly to vacation windows; agree blackout dates with faculty; build programme float; consider out-of-hours working where permitted.

riskRegister.description: Restricted working hours (Q3.5) extend construction duration and may attract premium labour or out-of-hours rates, increasing cost and programme risk.
riskRegister.mitigation: Confirm permitted hours with the client; price out-of-hours working where programme-critical; reflect in Preliminaries.

riskRegister.description: The site is in a conservation area or subject to an Article 4 direction (Q3.8); permitted development rights are curtailed and external alterations are likely to require full planning consent, with potential for enhanced material and detailing requirements.
riskRegister.mitigation: Seek pre-application advice on the conservation officer's expectations; assume full planning for external works when programming; allow for enhanced material specification in the cost plan at Stage 2.

riskRegister.description: Asbestos is known or suspected (Q3.1); survey and safe removal add cost and programme risk, particularly given the building's age (1960s) and the full systems replacement scope.
riskRegister.mitigation: Obtain a current asbestos register and condition survey; confirm scope and cost of removal; allow contingency for unforeseen asbestos-containing materials during strip-out.

riskRegister.description: The building has life-expired M&E services with no replacement since original construction (Q3.1); full systems replacement is required, creating uncertainty in hidden condition and potential for scope growth.
riskRegister.mitigation: Commission a detailed M&E condition survey at Stage 2; establish a robust change control process; allocate adequate contingency for unforeseen defects.

riskRegister.description: The target date of 1 September 2028 is not achievable from the stated start of 11 January 2027; the 124-week programme completes around 28 May 2029, approximately 38 weeks beyond target.
riskRegister.mitigation: Confirm realistic target date with the client; explore acceleration options (long-lead procurement, survey reuse) at Stage 2; consider phasing to deliver priority spaces earlier.

riskRegister.description: Multiple phases are planned with re-mobilisation costs and programme gaps; phase split is not yet confirmed (Q4.6), creating uncertainty in total cost and delivery schedule.
riskRegister.mitigation: Define phase boundaries and re-mobilisation strategy at Stage 2; confirm which spaces are priority; establish clear handover and occupation protocols between phases.

aiProse.procurementNarrative: A Traditional Single Stage Tender route with JCT Standard Building Contract 2024 is appropriate for this refurbishment of known scope, where the client design team will develop the detailed specification during Stage 2 and the contractor will price and deliver against a fixed specification. This route delivers the client's priority for fixed and certain final cost, as the contractor's price is locked at tender stage, and suits the formal competitive procurement required by the grant funding source regardless of project value.
procurementConsiderations: Long-lead procurement of major plant (switchgear, air handling units) should be explored at Stage 2 to reduce the critical path by 8–30 weeks; this requires early specification and client commitment to advance payment but may help recover the current 38-week programme shortfall against the target date.
The asbestos register must be validated as a current and scope-relevant R&D survey; if confirmed, it may be reused to remove the survey contingency and de-risk the programme by approximately 3 weeks.

Phasing strategy must be confirmed before tender to allow contractors to price re-mobilisation costs accurately and to establish clear blackout dates and occupation protocols that minimise disruption to teaching activities during term time.
